title: AI Attackers Don’t Wait for the Annual Pentest. Nor can Banks
snippet: Aikido Security's Selim Decamps argues banks facing AI-driven attackers must move from annual pentests to continuous AI testing inside their own data centres. The post AI Attackers Don’t Wait for the Annual Pentest. Nor can Banks appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Attackers can now point a cheap AI model at a bank’s systems and leave it probing around the clock, while most banks still test their defences on an annual cycle. A security engineer argues the answer is continuous AI pentesting that runs inside the bank’s own walls, so code and data never leave the building.

Selim Decamps, Aikido machine lead engineer at Aikido Security

Selim Decamps is the Aikido machine lead engineer at Aikido. Previously, he was the founder of Milou. In this contributed piece he sets out why banks need to move from periodic to continuous security testing, and how they can do so without sending code or data outside their networks. The views are his own.

A bank can spend millions on its security infrastructure. Meanwhile, someone with a ChatGPT subscription that costs ten pounds can set up an AI model to probe that same system for vulnerabilities and leave it running indefinitely. Today’s attackers do not even need to know what they are doing. The AI does the work, and it keeps going without breaks, without losing focus and without stopping when it hits a dead end. Financial services organisations are not yet ready for that volume of attacks.

European regulators are, unsurprisingly, concerned. In July, the European Central Bank gave major banks four months to produce action plans against AI-driven cyber threats. The Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) already requires annual testing of critical information and communications technology (ICT) systems, as well as threat-led penetration testing on live production systems for the most significant institutions.

But keeping up with AI-powered attackers probing at all hours means banks need to test far more often to keep their systems secure.

AI pentesting for continuous coverage

Banks have pentested their defences the same way for more than two decades. They hire a team of human security experts to attack an agreed set of systems over a few weeks, then wait for a report. By the time those results arrive, the code in production may already be many versions ahead.

AI pentesting changes the timeline completely. AI agents learn how an application is supposed to behave, then try to break it the way an attacker or human pentester would. They work in parallel across an application, cutting weeks of manual work down to hours. In our own benchmark against external manual pentests, AI testing took roughly eight to 14 hours per web application, while the human pentests ran from eight days to four weeks.

Even though AI pentesting is already producing high-quality results, banks have been slow to adopt it because most of it runs in the cloud. The deepest testing is white-box, where the agents need source code and system context, and in a cloud set-up both travel to a vendor’s servers and through an external AI model. Black-box testing avoids sharing code, but it gives up depth, and the data the agents see still passes through the vendor’s infrastructure.

For most banks that ends the conversation, since policy often says code and privileged data cannot leave the network. DORA requires banks to know where their data is stored and processed at all times, and it treats outside technology providers, AI included, as third-party risk to be managed.

Data residency concerns

When 400 security and engineering leaders were asked which technical controls a system must enforce before they would accept AI pentesting, data residency guarantees, cited by 38 per cent, ranked in the top two. Until now, banks have handled data residency concerns by running security testing on-premises. Dynamic application security testing (DAST) tools and vulnerability scanners, for example, can easily run inside the network.

But those tools are limited when it comes to finding complex vulnerabilities, and they mostly stop at detection. They cannot reason about how an application is supposed to behave, which means they miss business logic flaws, broken access control and multi-step attack chains in which small individual issues combine into something serious. AI pentesting agents can find these, and can run further validation on each finding to rule out false positives and hallucinations, so only verified findings, with their impact and reproduction steps, make it into the report.

What banks need, then, is AI pentesting that keeps code and privileged data inside the network.

Fortunately, open-weight AI models are now both capable enough for serious testing and small enough to run on a single server without an internet connection, so AI pentesting can live almost anywhere. On-premises deployment combines the power and accuracy of AI pentesting with the data residency benefits of running on the bank’s own hardware.

Belfius, the bank-insurer owned by the Belgian federal government with EUR 192.8bn in assets, is already working this way. Aikido has deployed air-gapped AI pentesting inside the bank’s own data centre, where more than 200 AI agents now test its systems regularly. Source code and findings never leave the building, and Aikido has no access to the bank’s data.

From periodic to continuous testing

Once the AI lives inside the bank, testing can run non-stop. Because the bank owns the hardware, its security teams do not have to ration pentests or wait weeks for them, and AI agents can test each software release as it ships.

Fabian Delava, head of technology at Belfius, has described cybersecurity as no longer a periodic exercise but a continuous mission, saying that agents testing the bank’s systems around the clock let it identify risks faster and strengthen its resilience continuously.

DORA’s testing requirements are one way banks prove their resilience, and continuous pentesting inside their own infrastructure lets them meet those requirements without moving data elsewhere. Banks can use the same AI-driven security as everyone else. They may just have to bring it home.

title: Behind the Idea: Toden
snippet: Toden co-founder Charles Archibong on how fragmented verification, fraud and compliance tools in his own fintech led him to build an identity and risk platform. The post Behind the Idea: Toden appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Toden is an identity verification and risk-management software company that helps digital businesses verify people and businesses, assess risk and monitor activity through an API and dashboard.

Charles Archibong, co-founder of Toden

In this Behind the Idea, Charles Archibong, co-founder of Toden, explains how running into fragmented verification, fraud and compliance tools while building a fintech led to the company, and why the work between the checks matters as much as the checks themselves.

Tell us more about your company and its offering

Toden is an identity verification and risk-management software company. We help digital businesses verify people and businesses, screen for sanctions and other risks, and connect those checks to decisions and ongoing monitoring. Teams use an API and dashboard, with SDKs and hosted verification links for collecting information. A developer can test the integration in a free sandbox before paying for production checks.

What problem was your company set up to solve?

We encountered fragmented verification, fraud and compliance tools while building a fintech. Each tool could do its own job, but we still had to connect the results to the customer’s journey. Who reviews an uncertain result? What should they see? How does their decision reach the application, and what happens when a new signal appears later? That work between the checks became the reason for building Toden. We are keeping the earlier fintech and its customers unnamed.

Since launch, how has your company evolved?

The original problem continues to shape the product. Verification is part of a longer relationship with a customer, so the product needs to connect onboarding with review and ongoing monitoring. You can see that approach today in the workflows, dashboard and integration tools. Our emphasis is on making the whole process usable by the people responsible for it, including the situations where a check is uncertain or someone needs to step in.

What has been the biggest challenge or most ‘tricky moment’ to overcome?

The difficult part has been thinking beyond a successful check. A developer needs a clear result, an operations team needs enough context to review a case, and the person waiting needs to understand the next step. Those responsibilities meet in the same journey. The fragmentation we experienced made that a central design problem for us.

What are your biggest achievements or ‘proudest moment’ so far?

For me, it is turning a problem we encountered as builders into a product another team can examine and test. The free sandbox matters because people should be able to explore the integration and its different outcomes before committing production spending. That is a concrete way to show our thinking and let teams decide whether it fits their own responsibilities.

How would you describe the culture of your company?

The culture I want us to build centres on care and clear ownership. A person sharing an identity document deserves a process they can understand. A reviewer needs evidence they can follow, and a developer needs to know what happens when something is delayed or uncertain. I want those questions to stay part of product decisions, with room to say what we do not yet know and test it properly.

What’s in store for the future?

Our direction is to keep improving the connections between verification, risk decisions and the work that follows onboarding. We want the developer experience to be easier to evaluate and the review process clearer to operate. We will keep sharing what we build and listening to the teams doing that work.

title: Adyen co-founder to step down
snippet: “I feel my cycle is complete,” Pieter van der Does, also co-CEO, wrote after 20 years with Adyen. “This is the right moment for me to step down.”
fullText:
Dive Brief:

Pieter van der Does, co-founder and co-chief executive of the payment processor Adyen, will step down Dec. 31 and move to an advisory role, the Amsterdam-based company said Monday.

Van der Does will hand the reins to co-CEO Ingo Uytdehaage, who has been with the company since 2011.

“We have been planning this transition for more than three years with the Co-CEO model,” van der Does said Monday in an open letter posted to LinkedIn. “It took some time for all the pieces to fall into place, but the moment is now.”

Dive Insight:

Van der Does, a Dutch billionaire, founded the company in November 2006 with Arnout Schuijff, with whom he previously worked at Dutch payment processor Bibit Global Payment Services. Adyen works with merchants including Uber, McDonald’s and eBay.

Under van der Does, who was Adyen’s sole CEO until 2023, the firm grew to €12.26 billion ($13.44 billion) in assets by Dec. 31, 2025, when it last announced its full-year financial statement. 

For the third quarter this year, net revenue was €738.1 million ($809.6 million), up 23% year-over-year, while total processed volume was €451.1 billion ($494.8 billion), up 30% year over year, according to the company’s quarterly report.

Still, the company’s profit margins are expected to edge down this year to 50%, according to the third-quarter report, from 53% for 2025, even though Adyen forecast last year that margins would be expected to rise to 55% by 2028. Adyen has faced pricing pressures in the processing realm as competition has increased from established players, like PayPal Holdings and Fiserv, as well as other fintechs, such as Stripe and Shift4 Payments.

Adyen’s depository shares trading in the U.S. have had a price drop so far this year of about 44%.

Meanwhile, the company has been adjusting to management turnover, including installing an interim chief financial officer, and changing its leadership in the U.S., where it has been seeking to expand. “Reflecting the momentum in the business, our recent hiring has been focused on specialized technical and go-to-market roles, particularly in the US,” the company said in the third-quarter update.

“Adyen outgrew our wildest imagination,” van der Does wrote in his letter. “I never thought it would lead us to where we are today: global, innovative and strong … Adyen went through many iterations and there are many new iterations to come.”

Building Adyen “has been an honour. This moment also marks 20 years for me as (Co-)CEO, and I feel my cycle is complete,” he wrote. “This is the right moment for me to step down, on a positive note and with a very good feeling.”

Van der Does expressed “full trust” in Uytdehaage, the board, and the global leadership team moving forward.

Uytdehaage joined the company as CFO in 2011 and held the role until 2023, when he was named co-CEO.

“Pieter built more than a company. He built a culture that shapes how we make decisions, how we treat each other and how we put our merchants first, and it will outlast any one of us,” Uytdehaage said in a press release.

“I’ve had the privilege of building Adyen alongside him for more than 15 years. I’m grateful for what he has given the company, and our job now is to keep building on what he started. I look forward to executing on the strategy we built together.”

Van der Does has outlasted Schuijff’s tenure at the company, which ended in 2020. Schuijff left to found hospitality management and payment platform Tebi, according to his LinkedIn profile.

Lynne Marek contributed to this story.

title: Premialab and Aladdin Partner on QIS Analytics for Institutions
snippet: Premialab's QIS data platform will integrate with BlackRock's Aladdin to give institutional investors holdings-level transparency and risk attribution for systematic The post Premialab and Aladdin Partner on QIS Analytics for Institutions appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Premialab, the independent quantitative investment strategy (QIS) data platform, has announced a partnership with Aladdin, BlackRock‘s investment management operating system, to bring specialist QIS analytics directly into the workflows of their shared institutional clients. The integration, announced on 2 November 2026, pairs Premialab’s factor attribution and scenario analysis capabilities with Aladdin’s risk infrastructure and broad institutional reach.

Adrien Géliot, CEO at Premialab

The practical output is threefold. Common clients will gain holdings-level transparency across QIS strategies sitting within wider multi-asset portfolios, granular risk attribution identifying the return drivers of each strategy, and continuous data quality management sourced from 20 leading QIS banks. For institutions already running Aladdin as their central operating system, the benefit is consolidation: QIS exposures will be modelled and monitored through the same infrastructure they use for the rest of the book, rather than via a separate, disconnected process.

Kamya Somasundaram, global head of Aladdin Enterprise Partnerships at BlackRock

Premialab chief executive Adrien Géliot described the deal as addressing “a longstanding operational challenge that has constrained QIS adoption,” pointing to connectivity gaps and operational friction as the primary barriers. Kamya Somasundaram, global head of Aladdin enterprise partnerships at BlackRock, said clients were seeking “greater depth and precision in how these strategies are modelled, monitored and reported.”

Why the operational plumbing matters

QIS have moved from a niche structured-products category into mainstream institutional portfolio construction over the past decade, but their adoption has consistently run ahead of the back-office infrastructure designed to support them. Unlike vanilla equity or fixed-income positions, QIS are composite exposures that blend factor tilts, volatility overlays and derivative structures in ways that resist standard attribution frameworks. Institutions holding QIS alongside traditional assets have often managed them in siloed systems, creating reconciliation problems, incomplete risk pictures and reporting inconsistencies that compliance and risk teams find difficult to resolve.

Premialab’s dataset, which the company says processes more than 15 million data points daily across over 8,000 investable systematic strategies and represents approximately 20 trillion US dollars in client assets under management, is built to address precisely this gap. The Aladdin partnership gives that dataset distribution at institutional scale: Aladdin is used by pension funds, insurers, sovereign wealth funds and asset managers across most major markets, making it one of the more consequential platforms to which a specialist analytics provider can connect.

The integration is well-timed relative to the regulatory environment. Under Solvency II and its UK post-Brexit equivalent, UK Solvency Reform, insurers face detailed reporting obligations on derivatives and structured exposures that make robust QIS attribution a compliance necessity, not merely a risk-management preference. Similarly, the EU’s AIFMD II requirements, which took effect in 2024, tighten reporting expectations for alternative strategies held by institutional funds, adding further pressure on the data quality and audit trail that a Premialab-Aladdin integration can support.

Premialab operates in a segment where several asset managers and index providers have built proprietary QIS analytics, but few independent platforms offer the breadth of bank coverage it claims across 20 counterparties. The Aladdin partnership reinforces a distribution moat: institutions that standardise their operating environment on Aladdin will find switching to a competing analytics layer costly, which lengthens the commercial relationship for Premialab. The next milestones to watch are client adoption numbers, the jurisdictions in which the integration launches first, and whether the deal expands to cover Aladdin’s eFront private-markets module, where QIS overlays are increasingly used by infrastructure and credit funds.

title: Intermex sues Western Union
snippet: The long-time remittance provider walked away from a $500 million merger deal due to “buyer’s remorse,” Intermex alleged in a Tuesday lawsuit.
fullText:
Dive Brief:

International Money Express sued Western Union on Tuesday seeking to enforce the terms of its $500 million merger agreement that Western Union abandoned earlier this month. Western Union contracted “a bad case of buyer’s remorse” over the 2025 deal as the remittance business deteriorated, according to the lawsuit.

Western Union gained at least $50 million in annual cost savings and financial improvements by studying Intermex’s operations during the merger planning period, according to the lawsuit. “By walking away, Western Union got that value at the expense of Intermex’s stockholders without having to pay those stockholders a dime,” Intermex said in the lawsuit filed in Delaware.

Western Union “stands by its decision to terminate the merger agreement and strongly disagrees with the claims asserted by Intermex in its lawsuit,” a spokesperson said Tuesday in an email. “We believe we acted in accordance with the terms of the merger agreement and intend to vigorously defend against the lawsuit.”

Dive Insight:

The lawsuit filed in the Delaware Court of Chancery alleges breach of contract by Western Union for not completing the deal, and seeks to enforce the merger agreement, along with injunctive relief and damages.

“Intermex believes Western Union’s purported termination is invalid given that all conditions to the closing have been satisfied,” the company said Tuesday in a press release.

The merger deal dates to August 2025, when Western Union agreed to pay $16 per share for Miami-based Intermex, which was founded in 1994 and enables money transfers from the U.S. and four other countries to about 60 nations, with a network of thousands of bank and retail locations.

Denver-based Western Union, which provides cross-border payments services and has roots reaching back more than 100 years, provides remittance services at locations worldwide.

On Aug. 14, the California Department of Financial Protection and Innovation – which had earlier approved the transaction – suspended an approval it had granted only two weeks before. That decision occurred the same day New York regulators approved the merger, with conditions.

Intermex said Western Union “seized” on the August California DFPI decision “as an opportunity to escape the deal and abscond with hundreds of millions of dollars in synergies, while leaving Intermex a wounded company,” according to the lawsuit. “Rather than using its reasonable best efforts to fix the problem in California, Western Union sat on its hands and let the clock run.”

The company had “insisted on control of the regulatory process,” Intermex said in the lawsuit, but failed to engage in constructive talks with the California agency, which is led by Rohit Chopra, the former director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. The DFPI approved the merger, with conditions, on Nov. 10. 

“Western Union deliberately stalled, offering nothing and leaving it to DFPI to propose conditions on its own, knowing that every day of delay brought it closer” to the Nov. 10 date, which permitted termination of the agreement if the deal had not closed.

However, Western Union CEO Devin McGranahan “met privately with Secretary Chopra, without Intermex, in discussions that, upon information and belief, addressed whether the $16 price was too high,” Intermex said in the lawsuit.

McGranahan also held a town hall meeting on Oct. 13 with Intermex employees and said the Nov. 10 closing date would be extended if necessary, according to the lawsuit.

The remittance business has been turbulent over the past two years amid U.S. changes in immigration policies under the Trump administration, plus the longer-running industry shift from physical money-remittance stores to digital channels.

Last year, remittances to Mexico – the largest remittance recipient in the Americas – fell for the first time in 11 years, declining about 4% to $62.5 billion, according to the lawsuit.

These changes were caused by reduced migrant workers in the U.S., “which multiple industry analysts have attributed as a significant factor in declining remittances,” Intermex said in the suit. Intermex also cited a 1% excise tax on remittances the U.S.  imposed on Jan. 1, along with the industry move from retail to digital channels.

“Western Union came under intense pressure from its stockholders to find a way to escape from the deal it had agreed to a year earlier,” the lawsuit said.

Cross-border payments company Payoneer Global has received conditional regulatory approval to form its national trust bank, PAYO Digital Bank, nine months after submitting its application to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

PAYO Digital Bank, once approved, plans to issue its own stablecoin, PAYO-USD, which will serve as a balance within the Payoneer ecosystem. It will not be listed on exchanges.

“It allows us to give our customers a more seamless experience when they engage across stablecoin, fiat, and in the markets they operate,” Rob Morgan, PAYO Digital Bank’s proposed CEO, told Banking Dive in an interview Monday. “By issuing our own token, we can move customers into that Payoneer-issued balance in real time, which then gives them the ability to use that last mile in the markets where they run and operate their business.”

As PAYO Digital will hold the reserves that back PAYO-USD, “we can use that to facilitate payouts in the markets where those customers operate and make that stablecoin balance more useful in the real world,” Morgan said.

Stablecoins, he said, allow for global money movement in a way that lets business owners focus on running their business “as opposed to thinking about payments.”

PAYO Digital customers will be able to hold their PAYO-USD balances in approved digital wallets, and businesses will be able to pay or be paid in a number of third-party stablecoins and to convert balances into local fiat.

One-third of Payoneer’s customers already use stablecoin today, according to Morgan.

With conditional approval secured, PAYO Digital is building out its platform and working toward its opening exam, Morgan said.

The conditional approval is “a validation of what we have both built to date, the strength of Payoneer's business, the strength of our compliance, as well as the vision for where this is going, and we're excited to be building what we think is the future of global money movement,” Morgan said.

Payoneer is in the midst of an acquisition process: By mid-2027, it’s set to become a subsidiary of Canadian payments processor Nuvei, which said in June it would acquire Payoneer for $2.75 billion to build a bigger cross-border commerce business.

Morgan declined to comment on how the deal would impact PAYO Digital, noting that at this time, Payoneer and Nuvei continue to operate as independent companies.

title: Fed president pitches FedNow
snippet: Jeff Schmid, who leads the Kansas City Federal Reserve, nudged credit union executives last week to adopt faster payment options, like FedNow.
fullText:
The Federal Reserve has been trying to increase adoption of its FedNow instant payments system, and some regional Fed bank leaders are taking up the campaign.

Kansas City Federal Reserve Bank President Jeff Schmid addressed the issue in a speech last week at a National Credit Union Management Association conference. While he talked mainly about the economy, he devoted a significant chunk of the address to encouraging the credit union audience to consider adopting faster payment practices.

“Why do instant payments matter now?” he asked attendees, according to the text of his speech, delivered to the group in Hawaii on Nov. 15. “Because the market has changed.”

Today, 78% of consumers “prefer faster payments when given the option” and 66% of businesses “are likely to use instant payments if their financial institution offers them,” Schmid said, citing Fed research. 

Real-time payment systems, like FedNow, allow payments to move within seconds, as opposed to days for some legacy systems. FedNow is also available for use around the clock and on weekends. While that makes such systems more expedient to use, it also presents difficulties if an errant payment needs to be reversed.

Federal Reserve officials have been trying hard to persuade U.S. banks and credit unions to sign up for FedNow since it launched in July 2023, just weeks before Schmid took office the following month. The system is available only to financial institutions in the U.S.

FedNow adoption by financial institutions has been slow-going. In September, the Fed announced it would offer a discount on FedNow fees, starting Jan. 1, 2027, seemingly to spur more interest. Nonetheless, only those enrolled in certain Fed service programs and meeting specified FedNow volume thresholds, are eligible for reduced fees.

Currently, about 2,000 of the approximately 8,400 financial institutions in the U.S. are FedNow participants. That means only about a quarter of the ever-consolidating industry has signed up to be part of the Fed’s faster payments system over the past three years. 

That could be partly because the private sector had already created a real-time payments system in the form of the RTP network in 2017, giving it a first-mover advantage in attracting banks and credit unions. 

With RTP owned by The Clearing House, which is in turn owned by some of the largest banks in the world, FedNow was expected to have more appeal for smaller financial institutions that might not want to join a network owned by their larger rivals. 

How big banks use FedNow

Many of the major U.S. banks, including seven of the ten biggest, also participate in FedNow, giving them a back-up system for faster payments.

For instance, Capital One Financial isn’t interested in “picking a winner” between FedNow and RTP, but rather using both in case one system has a hiccup, said Capital One Managing Vice President Avik Chatterjee, who oversees payments at the bank. He has observed that other banks are doing the same, he said in an interview last month.

“What we want to strive for is, give the redundancy of real-time rails for our customers,” Chatterjee said. “We definitely want to participate on both the rails.”

While the big banks account for the majority of the volume that passes over FedNow, Schmid noted that smaller financial institutions – those with less than $10 billion in assets – make up 95% of FedNow participants.

Still, Schmid presented statistics that show credit unions aren’t necessarily keen to engage with FedNow. Only about 600 credit unions, of some 4,200 in the country, had joined FedNow as of the end of July, equal to about one in seven credit unions nationwide, he said.

“There is room to grow, but the momentum is real,” he observed. “Credit union participation is up more than 40% year-over-year.”  

He emphasized that more participation is important because the benefit of the system grows with more endpoints. “A payment network becomes more valuable with every institution that joins, and especially with every institution that can both send and receive,” Schmid said.

Use cases for instant payments that have been gaining ground over the past few years include quick payments to workers through earned wage access services. Also, because real-time systems operate around-the-clock, they are useful for the settlement of transactions that sometimes take place on weekends, like auto loans for the purchase of a car.

It makes sense for consumers and businesses to embrace faster payments, partly because such payments lower risks associated with slower settlement, especially for small businesses that crave price certainty, Schmid said.  “Faster access to funds improves liquidity for households and businesses,” he said.

However, of the financial institutions that have chosen to be a part of FedNow, many are hedging their risks by signing up just to receive real-time transactions, but not to send real-time payments. That means they can collect those payments without letting them flow out.

Using FedNow to counter fraud threats

The Kansas City Fed president painted a picture of instant payments being more insulated from fraud risks than some other forms of payment, namely paper checks. 

With that comment he was likely trying to counter a concern that banking and financial professionals have had since the advent of real-time payments: That faster payments would result in faster fraud. 

It’s an issue that Matt Clark, who is the chief revenue officer for business-to-business payments at the check and fintech company Deluxe, heard industry counterparts talking about earlier this month at the Association for Financial Professionals industry conference. While those professionals are eager to participate in faster payments, they’re balancing that desire with caution related to fraud, he said.

“We'll obviously continue to shift towards faster payments, but there is still that risk of increasing your fraud numbers by allowing that faster payment,” Clark said in an interview Thursday. 

Schmid urged the listeners in the audience to consider how they might “offer speed without sacrificing safety.” In addition to security tools built into FedNow that use historical data to spot problematic patterns in real-time, the system lets financial institutions control how they use the system, he said.

“On the sending side, you set your own limits, your own controls, and your own hours, based on what fits your members and your operational capacity,” Schmid said. “What you commit to is being ready to receive, around the clock, so that when someone sends your member money, it arrives.”

Further touting FedNow’s protections, he said the Fed is working with the private sector to keep improving FedNow’s risk management features.

“Efficient and safe payments are the circulatory system of the economy,” Schmid said. “When money flows reliably, other products and services can deliver their full value. When it doesn't, even the most thoughtful lending program or polished mobile app will be constrained.”

title: The Benefits of AI in Finance
snippet: AI is reshaping finance across transactional, analytical and strategic roles, but its value will depend on automating the right tasks while strengthening human judgement, accountability and financial controls. The post The Benefits of AI in Finance appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Are we getting the benefits of AI in Finance back-to-front?

Are we in danger of automating the wrong layer?

I spent the earlier part of this year reading and thinking about what is at stake with AI in Finance. I would not dare to say I have unveiled the secrets of the philosopher’s stone. Yet, I am wondering how much we are getting it backward. Let me explain myself.

Most debates about AI in Finance today still start with the threatening, not to say petrifying question : “Which finance jobs will be replaced?”.

Let’s be honest, it is (purposedly?) scary. One feels like he is in a gigantic musical chairs game. Hopefully, it is not as bad as it sounds.

That said, there is a real shift and this shift is more structural: AI is compressing execution-heavy finance tasks while reinforcing the need for strengthened layers where judgment, accountability, control and trust matter most.

In practice, the finance function seems on the cusp of splitting into three layers.

1.Transactional finance is highly automatable. AP, AR, invoice processing, reconciliations, standard journal entries and close checklists are high-volume, rule-based processes. It’s predictable and the Finance community has not waited for AI to engage on such path. Simply put, automation will keep driving efficiency here.

2.Analytical finance is being redesigned. FP&A, reporting, forecasting and variance analysis will not disappear. But the work is shifting: there is much less time spent preparing data and building models. And much more time dedicated to challenging assumptions, interpreting signals and aligning decisions across the business. In that respect, AI is not as great as it might seem at first but it will definitively have an impact on various pieces, not as a global system.

The most interesting sign is how Financial Planning & Analysis (FP&A) is moving from an analyst function to a decision-interface function.

3.Strategic finance will be reinforced. CFOs, controllers, treasury leaders, tax specialists, investor relations and corporate development are all operating in areas where outputs are not just calculated. They are owned, defended, audited and externally validated. In that respect, tweaking an old saying, I would say that he who lived by AI will die by AI. For one reason : AI can support these roles massively. But AI cannot assume any responsibility for them.

But let push it one step further.

The risk for finance leaders is not under-automation. Instead, it is automating the wrong layer. If an AI output is not explainable, auditable and controllable, it is not finance-grade. And speed without judgement and traceability is not productivity … it is risk.

This is why the performance of AI in finance will depend less on the model itself than on the financial control layer underneath. It will go beyond this too to incorporate structured data, clear ownership, continuous controls, audit trails and evidence that can be trusted. Hopefully technical solutions already exist to do it in a safe way.

The workforce impact will therefore be uneven:

1.Demand will decline for repetitive processing and data-preparation roles. Those that have such skills usually also have the understanding and the ability to level up and prepare their own personal shift. At least, they should be thinking about doing this.

2.Demand will rise for finance business partners, transformation leads, strategic controllers and finance data architects.

The finance function is not being eliminated. It is being reorganised based on what I would label as ‘cognitive value’. Low judgment tasks will be automated, medium judgment will be fairly augmented, and for high judgement & accountability responsibility will need to be reinforced.

At the end of the day, for CFOs, the new differentiator is not how much AI they deploy as a trophy.

The finance function does not create value by producing faster numbers on their own. It creates value by producing faster numbers the business, auditors and regulators can trust. AI will amplify that value only when it is built on finance-grade foundations, i.e. reliable data, continuous controls, traceable decisions and auditable evidence.

Will write to affected consumers, explaining that they do not have an enforceable obligation to make payment at this stage. (This means they do not need to pay now while regulatory and legal issues relating to the purported loans are resolved.)

Will not make further demands for payment from affected consumers in the current proposed court claim while regulatory and legal issues are resolved.

Additionally, Ethica and West 28 will not ask a court to make a judgment against someone who has not responded to a legal claim. This is known as a ‘default judgment’.  

However, consumers should not ignore any formal court documents they receive on this issue. They should consider seeking independent legal or debt advice before deciding what to do.

Additional protections for vulnerable consumers are being put in place and Ethica will identify affected consumers who may be vulnerable.

It has not yet been decided whether the debts can be enforced, which may be decided by a court.  

The requirements agreed protect consumers from avoidable harm while the relevant regulatory and legal issues are resolved.  

Consumers should not be subject to undue pressure when being contacted about a debt. If you believe you have been subjected to this type of behaviour, you should report it to us.

title: PayPal’s new CFO lands big pay
snippet: The digital payments player handed Claire Bramley, an HP alum, a $30 million pay package to take the chief financial officer post in February.
fullText:
Dive Brief:

Incoming PayPal CFO Claire Bramley is set to receive more than $30 million in stock awards and bonus compensation upon taking the top finance seat for the payments provider in February, according to a Friday regulatory filing. She will succeed Jamie Miller, who has served as PayPal’s CFO since 2023, and become CFO on Feb. 1, according to a Friday press release announcing the move.

PayPal is set to grant Bramley a one-time cash sign-on bonus of $5 million, payable in two installments contingent upon her continued employment with the company, according to the filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The company said it will also grant Bramley restricted stock units with a target grant value of $6 million, a sign-on RSU award with a value of $14 million, and a grant of performance-based RSUs with a grant date value of $6 million, according to the filing. In addition, Bramley’s compensation will include an annual base salary of $875,000, and she will be eligible to receive a target annual bonus of up to 125% of her base pay, according to the SEC filing.

Dive Insight:

The CFO transition is one of several executive moves announced Friday by the company, which in addition to its branded checkout service also owns and operates Venmo and Braintree.

Bramley will join fellow HP alum and PayPal CEO Enrique Lores at the San Jose, California-based company as it leans on a restructured leadership team as of this year to execute on a multi-year turnaround strategy.

Bramley is joining PayPal from financial software company Xero, where she has served as its CFO since June, according to her LinkedIn profile. Prior to Xero, which offers accounting software for small to midsize businesses, she served as CFO for Teradata. Her past experience also includes 14 years at technology company HP in roles such as global controller and finance leader for its Europe, Middle East and Africa division.

“What really attracted me to this role is the chance to help shape what’s next,” Bramley wrote in a Friday post on her LinkedIn profile announcing her move.” PayPal has played such an important role in transforming global commerce, and there’s so much more potential to unlock.”

Lores, formerly the CEO of HP, assumed PayPal’s top executive seat in March.

Since Lores took the seat, the payments provider has made numerous leadership transitions aimed at boosting profits and recovering consumer and investor attention. In April, he initiated the reorganization, with the company announcing it would be moving into a “simplified three business operating model,” according to a press release at the time. Those three areas include checkout Solutions & PayPal; consumer financial services & Venmo; and payment services & crypto.

On Friday, PayPal named Kartik Mani as its president and head of consumer financial services and Venmo; Suzan Kereere as president and head of payment services and crypto; and Juan Rio as executive vice president of AI business transformation and operations.

In another move, Brian Lee, formerly the chief risk officer for Goldman Sachs, joined the company’s board of directors — filling a vacancy created when it increased the size of its board from 11 to 12 members, PayPal said in a separate press release Friday.

The November appointments come after PayPal has “made significant progress in defining where we want to take PayPal and how we will compete and win,” Lores said in a statement included in the release.

“With our three-year strategies in place, our focus is now on execution,” he added. “These appointments bring together experienced leaders with the capabilities to accelerate innovation, strengthen our businesses and deliver greater value to our customers and shareholders.”

In its most recent earnings report Oct. 27, Lores touted PayPal’s progress but noted the company still has “more work to do.” The company reported increases in total payment volume and net revenue, according to its earnings release for the third quarter. Net income fell by about 14% year-over-year to about $1.1 billion, while earnings per diluted share inched down by 4% to $1.25.

Miller will step down from her current role as chief financial and operating officer effective as of Feb. 2 after a three-year tenure and a stint as its interim CEO in February — after then CEO and President Alex Chriss exited following an earnings miss and weak guidance, according to company filings and reports at the time.

Miller will receive severance payments and benefits applicable upon a termination without cause according to her separation agreement with the company, according to the Friday SEC filing.

PayPal will provide an update on its three-strategy progress during its fourth-quarter earnings report, the company said Friday.

title: How digital dollars improve cross-border payment management
snippet: As businesses look for more dependable ways to pay partners across borders, digital dollars are an emerging option.
fullText:
As businesses look for more dependable ways to pay suppliers and partners across borders, digital dollars — a form of internet-native money — are emerging as a practical option. 

Instead of hopping from bank to bank as each institution runs its own system, digital dollars allow money to move and settle on shared digital networks, just like how information moves across the internet. 

“Think of a digital dollar like an email,” said Meridith Perry, general manager of new business initiatives at Paystand. “It can be sent instantly and arrives within minutes. You see the status, so you know whether delivery failed or if it’s been opened. You can also attach information to it.”

With this infrastructure, senders and recipients access a shared payment record that details transaction amounts, send and receive dates and accompanying payment details so both sides can refer to that information whenever questions arise.

While adoption is early, finance teams that are putting digital dollars to work already report benefits, especially when it comes to cross-border payment operations. 

According to recent research from Paystand and CFO Dive’s Studio, financial leaders point to three ways digital dollars are improving international payments.

1. Payments Don’t Fail as Often

International payments moving along traditional rails pass through multiple banks and intermediary institutions, which makes failure hard to diagnose. This fragmentation puts finance teams at the mercy of updates that come from parties outside their control.

When an international payment fails or can’t be confirmed, the transaction can stall. This can cause 

Delays in critical business activities that depend on payments. While finance teams lose time on investigating settlement disputes and determining whether they need to resend funds, suppliers are left stalling as they await payment confirmation. 

When using digital dollars, however, 72% of users say fewer payments fail, are returned, or must be chased, research from Paystand and CFO Dive’s Studio found. Because they provide a direct, traceable record of payment with fewer handoffs, using digital dollars can mean less time spent tracking transactions and issuing repayments. This helps finance teams keep payments on track without manual follow-up.

2. Visibility into Payment Status Is Clearer 

To track a traditional international payment, status information is often split across sending banks, intermediary banks, receiving banks and payment providers. Once funds leave the sending bank, a  challenge arises. Finance teams often lack a direct, real-time view of an international payment’s progress. They have to ask their bank or the supplier for an update, which creates work. Those updates may arrive late or only during business hours, so they may already be out of date when the team receives them.

“The biggest challenge we hear about international payables is the lack of visibility or transparency,” Perry said. “This creates an operational-process burden: someone has to keep checking to see if payment arrived, or verify the payment amount.”

Because finance teams can’t tell where an international payment is in the process, suppliers, too, are in the dark as to when funds will arrive or if action needs to be taken to address a delay.

Digital-dollar users don’t have to piece together these updates as often: 56% report better visibility compared to previous payment methods, Paystand and CFO Dive’s Studio research found.

When using internet-native money, both parties use the shared record of activity created by the transaction to confirm whether a payment was sent, received or requires follow-up. This empowers finance teams to share updates with suppliers and stakeholders so both sides can plan around incoming funds and make sure problems don’t hold up other work.

“With traditional international payments, you may see two different numbers when you look at your bank compared to the other party’s bank,” Perry said. “But a shared transaction record gives both sides a common starting point: what moved, when it moved and whether the transfer was confirmed. When that record is connected to the invoice and accounting workflow, finance spends less time reconstructing what happened and can resolve exceptions sooner.”

3. Payments Are Completed Faster 

Slow payments can impact supplier relationships, time-sensitive purchases and access to funds, making it harder for businesses to secure the money they need and put it to work. And traditional cross-border payments are often held up due to factors like:

Bank cutoff times

Non-business days

Compliance reviews

Currency conversion

But nearly 1 in 3 respondents to the research from Paystand and CFO Dive’s Studio who use digital dollars say money arrives faster than with traditional payment methods. Digital-dollar networks operate continuously and often reduce the number of institutions involved in transactions. The result: Businesses can meet obligations on time and manage liquidity more responsively.

Perry pointed to a recent example.

“We worked with a business that held invoices for weeks to consolidate payments and pay one wire fee,” she said. “A more flexible payment process could let it pay sooner when that helps release an order. Payment timing should follow the needs of the business.”

The Cost of a Payment Is About More than Fees

“The transaction fee is only one part of the cost of a payment. Uncertainty creates work, ties up cash and delays decisions. The business case for digital dollars is whether they reduce those costs and give finance teams more control over when money becomes usable,” said Perry. “Digital dollars can reduce those demands.” 

Digital dollars give finance teams a clearer view of money in motion and more control over payment performance. For businesses that depend on suppliers and partners across borders, these benefits help keep payment issues from turning into business disruptions.

To learn more about what finance leaders are experiencing across payment operations and where things are headed by 2031, download the full report from Paystand.

title: Illinois fights for interchange law
snippet: The state’s attorney general filed a brief in appellate court Monday stressing the invalidity of a federal move to stop the Illinois Interchange Fee Prohibition Act.
fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                

The state’s attorney general filed a brief in appellate court Monday stressing the invalidity of a federal move to stop the Illinois Interchange Fee Prohibition Act.

        

            

        Published Nov. 25, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul speaks at a news conference on Aug. 25, 2025, in Chicago. His office is seeking to fend off federal efforts to preempt a state law meant to curb card interchange fees.
            
        
            Scott Olson via Getty Images
        
    
    
    

Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul pushed back Monday against Trump Administration agencies seeking to stop an Illinois law that would restrict card network interchange fees.

The state’s Interchange Fee Prohibition Act, signed into law in 2024, would limit fees charged by bank card issuers and card networks like Visa and Mastercard, disallowing the fees on taxes and tips. Interest groups representing the banks and credit unions that issue credit and debit cards sued the state to halt the law.

That battle between the state and bank groups has waged in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois since August 2024 when the Illinois Bankers Association, the American Bankers Association and other interest groups filed their lawsuit. The case is now before the 7th Circuit Court of Appeals after the lower court judge ruled in favor of the bank groups earlier this year, pointing to new federal rules that preempted the state law.

Interchange fees are charged to merchants, like retailers and restaurants, every time a consumer swipes a card to pay for a transaction. Merchant groups have been fighting the banks and card companies for decades, in court and in Congress, in an effort to lower the fees.

In an appellate court filing Monday, Raoul’s office reiterated the state’s prior arguments backing the soundness of the state’s law and countering U.S. District Court Judge Virginia Kendall’s ruling as “badly flawed.” 

Specifically, the AG contended that her decision was based on “invalid” federal rules that the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the National Credit Union Administration issued earlier this year in reaction to the Illinois law. The rules are invalid because the federal agencies didn’t follow proper procedures for issuing the regulations, Raoul’s office said. 

“OCC’s and NCUA’s interim final rules are invalid because the agencies failed to undertake notice-and-comment procedures before issuing them, and no ‘good cause’ justifies that failure,” the AG’s court filing said. 

Raoul also asserted Kendall’s contention that the state should have challenged the rules under the Administrative Procedure Act was faulty reasoning.

“That Illinois has not separately filed an APA action seeking vacatur of the rules is irrelevant because only a valid federal law can preempt a state law, and a federal regulation is invalid if it was not issued pursuant to the APA’s procedures,” the AG’s brief said. 

Spokespeople for the OCC and NCUA didn’t immediately respond to an emailed request for comment on the AG’s filing.

A coalition of nine trade associations in turn sued the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the National Credit Union Association this month over the agencies’ decision earlier this year to preempt the Illinois law.

fullText:
Credit cards are a useful financial tool for many – offering flexibility and helping people manage spending and cash flow.

But if customers only make low repayments over a long period, they can end up in debt for years while racking up interest and charges. 

The persistent debt rules we introduced in 2018 aimed to tackle this.

They said that lenders had to identify customers who, over an 18-month period, paid more in interest, fees and charges than towards their balance.

Lenders had to contact these customers and encourage them to increase repayments if they could afford it, and if they were still struggling, lenders had to take additional steps to help them repay their balances sustainably.

What changed for consumers

Our evaluation shows that consumer outcomes improved between 2018 and early 2023.  

Percentage of accounts in persistent debt

          

            						

We found that the proportion of credit card accounts in persistent debt fell by more than half between 2018 and early 2023, from 7% to 3%. Over the same period, monthly interest and fees for customers in persistent debt also fell.

Importantly, we found that many consumers changed their repayment behaviour after their provider contacted them.

In the 6 months after receiving their first persistent debt letter, over half of these customers raised their average repayments, around two-thirds reduced their average debt, and a majority reduced the proportion of their available credit they were using.

We also found that many customers moved out of persistent debt altogether. Of those who received an initial letter, more than half had left persistent debt within 18 months of receiving it, rising to almost two-thirds within 27 months.

These are encouraging signs. They suggest that clear communications and timely interventions can help those consumers who can afford to pay down their debt more quickly.

Supporting consumers who are struggling

However, these rules on their own can’t help all customers who may be really struggling.

Some simply aren’t able to pay more. Lenders need to do more than send communications: the earlier intervention rules we introduced at the same time as the persistent debt rules require firms to support consumers if they see signs of financial difficulty. The Consumer Duty also requires firms to act to prevent foreseeable harm.

Firms must understand their customers’ individual circumstances, communicate with them clearly and provide support such as reducing interest, fees or charges and directing people to free debt advice.

Our evaluation highlights the complexity of assessing outcomes in a changing economic environment.

The period covered by the research included the Covid-19 pandemic, the cost of living crisis, rising interest rates, and wider regulatory and market developments.  

So, although this means we can’t conclude that the persistent debt rules alone caused the improvements we observed, the consistency of the findings suggest the overall direction was positive in the period covered by our review.

Going forward, the new comprehensive data we collect from firms (product sales data) will help us to monitor the consumer credit market, including levels of persistent debt, and how changing economic conditions are affecting it.  

Credit card use and defaults have increased since the period covered by the evaluation. Initial analysis of recent product sales data suggests rates of persistent debt have risen, although it is still below the level it was at when we introduced the rules.

Help at the right time

One of the priorities in our strategy is helping consumers navigate their financial lives. To make this happen, firms need to ensure consumers receive good outcomes. Firms must support customers effectively, particularly when they are vulnerable or experiencing financial difficulty.

This evaluation suggests that the persistent debt framework can be an important part of achieving that goal.

There’s more to do. As household costs continue to rise, we’ll continue to monitor how firms support customers in persistent debt and ensure that those struggling with repayments receive the help they need at the right time.

Reducing persistent debt is not just about lowering balances and reducing the length of time it takes to pay off debt. It’s about helping consumers achieve better financial outcomes and become more financially resilient in the long term.

fullText:
How many of us read the terms and conditions of a contract before buying a financial product?

Contracts hold the detail that shapes everyone's financial life, whether you're taking out a loan, insuring your holiday, or signing up for a crypto wallet.

All firms are responsible for making sure that terms in their consumer contracts comply with the fairness and transparency requirements of the Consumer Rights Act (CRA) 2015. When those terms don’t comply, our Consumer Contracts team has powers to challenge firms directly.

This work shows how we use the full range of powers Parliament has given us, not only those in financial services legislation, to tackle harm.

Here's why it matters: if a term is found to be unfair, it's not just unenforceable – consumers may be due redress too. That's why it pays for firms to get this right from the start.

We review contract terms identified through our supervision of firms, information on social media, and referrals from consumers and other external stakeholders.  

When we take action  

We consider our rules and guidance, including the Consumer Duty, when deciding whether to act and which of our regulatory tools to use.  

Where we raise concerns about the fairness or transparency of terms, we expect firms to:  

Amend or delete the relevant terms so that the contract is fair and transparent, and stop relying on those terms in existing contracts.

Pay redress to consumers if the firm’s use of the terms has caused harm; and

In some cases, give us a voluntary undertaking under the CRA.  

Where necessary, we can apply for a court injunction to prevent a firm from using or enforcing the term against its customers. We can also seek a court order requiring it to pay redress.  

Examples of cases we've tackled

A crypto firm agreed to stop charging excessive storage fees which, in some cases, could exceed £40,000 a year. We intervened after finding it had charged inactive customers a disproportionate amount. The firm removed the term and paid redress to affected consumers.

A financial adviser updated its contracts after trying to charge a customer £800 for time spent handling a complaint. The charge was included in its terms and conditions, but we considered the term unfair because it could put people off making legitimate complaints. We also considered it inconsistent with the Consumer Duty and our own rules.

A travel insurer clarified unclear terms about what counted as a 12-hour delay and paid out £18,000 in redress to customers whose claims had been wrongly denied. Here, ambiguous wording was the problem, so we pushed for clearer terms that told consumers exactly what they were entitled to.

A lender improved the terms of a new credit product to give clearer information on costs and cancellation rights after we raised concerns ahead of launch. This is a good example of intervening early, through the authorisations process, to prevent unfair terms making it to market in the first place.

What we expect of firms

Firms should regularly check that their consumer contracts are fair, clear and transparent, and that they're being used fairly in practice.  

In practice, that means:

Taking into account consumers’ legitimate interests when designing contracts.

Using plain language, so customers understand what they're agreeing to: for example, what they might have to pay and what rights they have. Nobody should need a law degree to understand what they're signing up to.  

Avoiding surprises, by making important terms – fees, cancellation rights, variations, exclusions, complaints – easy to spot.

Reviewing contracts regularly to stay compliant with the latest requirements, rulings and judgments, and to learn from complaints, claims, cancellations, fees, customer outcomes and other data.

Testing whether customers actually understand key terms – not just assuming they do.

Improving staff training to ensure staff meet the standards set out in product literature, including contracts. Using complaints data to identify potentially unfair or unclear contract terms and make appropriate changes.

How to report concerns about unfair or unclear terms to us

Concerned about an unfair or unclear term in a financial services firm’s consumer contract? You can report it to us using our form. We can't always tell you what action we've taken, but, we can assure you, every report we receive gets considered.

title: Trump signs Common Cents bill
snippet: The new law gives merchants a legal basis for rounding retail cash transactions as pennies disappear.
fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                Dive Brief
        

                

The new law gives merchants a legal basis for rounding retail cash transactions as pennies disappear.

        

            

        Published Nov. 23, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                President Donald Trump signed legislation on November 20, 2026 that formally ends U.S. penny production and offers merchants a framework for rounding cash transactions.
            
        
            Getty Images
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

President Donald Trump signed the Common Cents Act into law on Friday, offering merchants a legal framework for rounding to the nearest nickel as the U.S. penny supply gradually dwindles.

The law – a top legislative priority for merchant trade groups – also formally ends production of the 1-cent coin, although the government stopped making it last year. Additionally, the measure authorizes the Treasury Department to research zinc as a copper replacement in the nickel to lower that coin’s 13-cent production cost.

With the law, “restaurant operators can have the confidence that they are handling cash transactions in a way that works for their business and for their customers,” Sean Kennedy, chief advocacy officer of the National Restaurant Association, said in a statement Friday. About 25% of restaurant purchases are still made with cash, Kennedy said.

Dive Insight:

The U.S. Mint announced in November 2025 that it had struck its final batch of pennies, nine months after Trump directed the U.S. Treasury to stop making the coin, citing their cost inefficiency. The department estimated $56 million in savings by ending penny production. 

Under the law, transactions that end with 1, 2, 6 or 7 cents would be rounded down to the nearest amount divisible by five; those ending with 3, 4, 8 or 9 cents in the sum are rounded up. Electronic transactions are excluded. 

Rep. Lisa McClain, a Michigan Republican who co-sponsored the House version with Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia of California, celebrated the signing Friday with a post on the social media site X. 

The legislation had two votes in both the House and Senate earlier this year due to an amendment added in the Senate version when that chamber endorsed the bill in August. The House passed the bill a second time on Sept. 14, followed by the Senate two weeks later.

“Washington was spending nearly four cents to make every one-cent penny,” wrote McClain, who is chair of the House Republican Caucus. “Not anymore. That’s what common sense, and Common Cents, looks like.”

The National Grocers Association hailed the new law as a solution for a problem its supermarket members confront daily.

“Independent grocers process millions of transactions every day, and the disappearance of the penny created a very practical problem at the checkout counter,” Stephanie Johnson, the association’s senior vice president and head of government affairs, said in a Friday press release. The law “provides the clarity and legal protections retailers need to handle cash transactions consistently and fairly.”

The Senate version of the legislation was co-sponsored by Cynthia Lummis, a Wyoming Republican, and Kirsten Gillibrand, a Democrat from New York.

“This is a Main Street issue, and there was unanimous agreement in both chambers on the final bill,” Brennan Duckett, director of regulatory and policy for NACS, the National Association of Convenience Stores, said in a press release. “It’s a good feeling knowing that this law removes a few of the hurdles that retailers face every day, and that we helped solve a real-world problem.”
